newsitem.title: UK: Britain's cash-rich BBC seeks further savings.
newsitem.headline: Britain's cash-rich BBC seeks further savings.

text.p: The British Broadcasting Corp. said Tuesday it had emerged from a deficit to post a cash surplus of $617 million as it prepares for the launch of new digital television services.
BBC Director-General John Birt said the government-run corporation set a target of boosting efficiency by a further 20 percent over the next five years.
The BBC plans to invest 9 percent of its revenue on its digital strategy and to plough $845 million into its existing network in the next five years.

The BBC, which derives most of its income from an annual license fee levied on all television households, has transformed its finances in the 1990s through cost savings and the sale of its transmission network.

"Together, these decisions were a historic breakthrough for the BBC, a vote of confidence in an organisation whose very nature, scope and survival were being questioned little more than a decade ago," Birt told reporters.

The BBC shed 1,700 employees in 1996-97 -- some 8 percent of its total staff. Birt refused to discuss the prospect of additional job cuts but said that a greater proportion of the staff would be employed in programme making.

Unions have criticised Birt in recent days after it was revealed his annual salary rose almost 20 percent last year to $598,000. But BBC Chairman Sir Christopher Bland said the salary was in line with the industry norm for media executives.
The BBC plans to launch a free 24-hour news channel next year as Britain introduces digital broadcasting which has extra channel capacity.
